items.title: The domination order on tableaux, Garnir tableaux and bricks
items.statement:
Retain English Young diagrams, an $l$-multicomposition $\mu$ of $d$, its
diagram, and the row-reading initial standard tableau $t^\mu$, in which
$1,2,\dots,d$ appear in order along the successive rows from top to bottom
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]); for a single
component this is the standard tableau of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]. A $\mu$-tableau $T$ is a
placement of $1,\dots,d$ in the nodes of $\mu$. It is **row-strict** if its
entries increase from left to right in every row of every component, and
**standard** if it is row- and column-strict. The group $S_d$ acts on tableaux
by its action on entries, and for a $\mu$-tableau $T$ the permutation $w_T$ is
defined by $w_Tt^\mu=T$. The **strong Bruhat order** on tableaux is
$$S\le_BT\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad w_S\le w_T$$
in the Bruhat order of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], identified
with its one-based realization as in
[[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]. We write $S\unlhd T$
for $S\le_BT$ and $S\lhd T$ for strict order; the separately declared meaning
of $\unrhd$ on partitions ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) is not
reused for tableaux. On row-strict $S,T$ the order $\unlhd$ is equivalent to
the prefix-shape comparison
$$\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le a})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le a})\quad\text{for every }a,$$
where $T^{\le a}$ erases the nodes occupied by entries $>a$ and
$\operatorname{sh}$ records the resulting row lengths read in row-reading
order; this row-sequence dominance is distinct from the weak Bruhat order and
must not be reversed. The transposition criterion is
$$S=(a_1\,b_1)\cdots(a_m\,b_m)T$$
with $a_n<b_n$ and $b_n$ occupying an earlier row-reading node than $a_n$ in
$(a_{n+1}\,b_{n+1})\cdots(a_m\,b_m)T$ for each $n$.

For entries $r,s$ of one component define $r\to_Ts$ if they lie in the same row
and $s$ is strictly to the right of $r$; $r\downarrow_Ts$ if they lie in the
same column and $s$ is strictly below $r$; and $r\nearrow_Ts$ if $s$ is
strictly above and strictly right of $r$ (south-west is the reverse of
$\nearrow_T$). A **weak Bruhat graph edge** $T\xrightarrow{r}S$ requires both
tableaux standard, $S=s_rT$, and $r$ occupying an earlier row-reading node
than $r+1$. Equivalently $r+1\nearrow_Tr$, or $r$ lies in an earlier component
than $r+1$. In particular a same-row or same-column swap is NOT a standard
edge. A **terminal path** is a directed path in this graph, and $T$ is
$(r_1,\dots,r_m)$-**terminal** if there are standard tableaux
$S_1\xrightarrow{r_1}S_2\xrightarrow{r_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{r_m}T$.

The **Garnir belt** at a node $(a,b,n)$ with $(a+1,b,n)$ also a node of $\mu$
consists of the nodes $(a,c,n)$ for $b\le c\le\mu_a$ and the nodes
$(a+1,g,n)$ for $1\le g\le b$. The **Garnir tableau** of shape $\mu$ at
$(a,b,n)$ is the unique maximal standard $\mu$-tableau in the order $\unlhd$
among the standard $\mu$-tableaux agreeing with $t^\mu$ outside the
$(a,b,n)$-Garnir belt; it equals $t^\mu$ in the degenerate case
$b=1=\mu_a$. A **horizontal brick** is a string of consecutive entries along
same-row right arrows. For the vertical exceptional-prefix and terminal assertions assume that
$\mu$ is a multipartition; the rank, prefix-order and row-sorting assertions
allow multicompositions. The following source facts are retained with these
exact conventions and are proved below: the transposition criterion and the
prefix-shape criterion; the row-strictness of a vertical consecutive swap and
its exceptional-prefix comparison; agreement outside the Garnir belt for
tableaux below a Garnir tableau; and the four terminal alternatives for a
horizontal or vertical consecutive pair, the last alternative being $t^\mu$
for a horizontal pair and the corresponding Garnir tableau for a vertical
pair. No choice.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An $l$-multicomposition $\mu$ of $d$, its row-reading initial
standard tableau $t^\mu$, the notions of row-strict and standard tableaux,
removable and addable nodes ([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]])
and partition dominance ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) for single
components, and the one-based permutation Bruhat order with its basic
properties. We prove the finite combinatorial facts displayed in the
Definition.

[F1] For a partition, tableaux are maps from the diagram with the standard
condition and the left action of $S_n$ as declared in
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]; extending componentwise
defines $\mu$-tableaux, row-strictness, standardness and the action used here.

[F2] Dominance of partitions of $n$ is the partial order by prefix sums,
$\lambda\unrhd\nu$ for all $k$, as declared in
[[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]; we use the same prefix-sum comparison
on row sequences of multicompositions.

[F3] Removable and addable nodes of a partition are as declared in
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]; a node $(a,b,n)$ with
$(a+1,b,n)$ a node lets us speak of a two-row belt.

[F4] Young diagrams, their English orientation and the nodes of a
multicomposition are as declared in
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

[F5] For $\sigma,\tau\in S_d$ the Bruhat order is the rank-inequality order
$r_\sigma(p,q)\ge r_\tau(p,q)$ for all $p,q$, identified with the one-based
realization by shifting inputs and values by $1$
([[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]]).

[F6] This order is the strong Bruhat order of type $A$: it is the transitive
closure of the covers $x\to tx$ with $t$ a transposition and
$\ell(tx)=\ell(x)+1$; it is graded by length, with every saturated chain from
$y$ to $w$ of length $\ell(w)-\ell(y)$; and $y\le w$ implies $\ell(y)\le\ell(w)$
with equality only for $y=w$
([[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **The permutation criterion.** Let $t=(a\ b)$ with $a<b$ act on values and write $p=x^{-1}(a)$, $q=x^{-1}(b)$. If $p<q$, direct inversion counting gives $\ell(tx)-\ell(x)=1+2\#\{j:p<j<q,\ a<x(j)<b\}>0$; if $p>q$ the difference is its negative. A positive difference need not equal one. The rank inequalities in [F5] show $x<tx$ precisely in the first case: the rank count decreases by one for $p\le h<q$ and $a\le k<b$, and is unchanged elsewhere. Thus every displayed earlier-node transposition lowers strong Bruhat order. Conversely a saturated strong-Bruhat chain from $w_S$ to $w_T$ consists of transposition covers by [F6], each of whose inverse lowering move has the earlier larger value by the formula just proved. Reading this chain backwards yields the displayed transposition criterion. [F5, F6, algebra]

1.2 **Agreement outside the Garnir belt.** In the row-reading initial labelling the two pieces of the belt form one contiguous interval of positions $[L,U]$: the upper-row tail is immediately followed by the lower-row prefix. A Garnir tableau changes labels only inside this interval, so $w_T$ is in the parabolic subgroup generated by $s_L,\ldots,s_{U-1}$. Sorting its interval permutation gives a reduced expression using only these generators. The Bruhat subword criterion applied to this expression says that every $w_S\le w_T$ likewise uses only these generators. Hence $w_S$ fixes all positions outside $[L,U]$, proving agreement with $t^\mu$ outside the belt. This applies even to nonstandard $S$. [F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 **The prefix-shape criterion.** For a row-strict $W$ and a value $c$, row-strictness makes the entries $\le c$ in each row a prefix, so $\operatorname{sh}(W^{\le c})$ is a row sequence of size $c$, and for $p=P_k+t$ with $P_k$ the number of nodes in the first $k$ rows and $0\le t<\mu_{k+1}$ we get $$N_W(p,c):=\#\{i\le p:\text{entry }i\text{ of }W\le c\}=A_k(W,c)+\min\bigl(t,s_{k+1}(W,c)\bigr),$$ where $A_k(W,c)$ is the number of entries $\le c$ in the first $k$ rows and $s_{k+1}(W,c)$ the prefix length in row $k+1$. By [F5], $w_S\le w_T$ iff $N_S(p,c)\ge N_T(p,c)$ for all $p,c$. At $p=P_k$ this says $A_k(S,c)\ge A_k(T,c)$ for all $k,c$, which is exactly $\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le c})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le c})$ for all $c$; hence the prefix criterion is necessary. Conversely assume all these prefix inequalities, fix $p=P_k+t$ and put $a=A_k(S,c)-A_k(T,c)\ge0$, $s=s_{k+1}(S,c)$, $s'=s_{k+1}(T,c)$; the inequality at $k+1$ gives $a+s\ge s'$. If $t\le s$ then $a+\min(t,s)=a+t\ge\min(t,s')$, because $t\le s'$ gives $a+t\ge t$ and $t>s'$ gives $a+t\ge t\ge s'$; if $t>s$ then $a+\min(t,s)=a+s\ge s'\ge\min(t,s')$. Thus $N_S(p,c)\ge N_T(p,c)$ for all $p,c$ and $S\unlhd T$. Since the first $k$ rows of $t^\mu$ contain $\min(c,P_k)$ entries $\le c$, the maximum possible, $\operatorname{sh}(t^{\mu\le c})$ dominates every $\operatorname{sh}(W^{\le c})$, so $t^\mu$ is the least element of $\unlhd$ on row-strict tableaux. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra, F2]

3.1 **Consecutive swaps and the edges of the weak graph.** Let $T$ be standard. If $r,r+1$ share a row, row-strictness puts $r$ immediately left of $r+1$ and the swap reverses an adjacent pair, so $s_rT$ is not row-strict; if they share a column, column-strictness puts $r$ immediately above $r+1$ and the swap reverses an adjacent column pair, so $s_rT$ is not column-strict. If in one component $r+1$ lies strictly above and strictly left of $r$, let $x$ be the entry of $T$ in the node in the row of $r$ and the column of $r+1$: row-strictness gives $x<r$ while column-strictness gives $x>r+1$, impossible, and symmetrically $r$ cannot lie strictly above and strictly left of $r+1$. The only remaining same-component configurations are $r\nearrow_Tr+1$ and $r+1\nearrow_Tr$; in either, the nodes sharing a row or column with the two positions are unchanged except for the interchange of the consecutive values $r,r+1$, so all strict neighbour inequalities survive and $s_rT$ is standard. If $r,r+1$ lie in different components the swap is standard as well. This proves the stated equivalence. For the edge criterion note that $S=s_rT$ with both standard and $r$ earlier than $r+1$ in $T$: in one component the alternatives of the equivalence leave only $r+1\nearrow_Tr$ (in the other alternative $r+1$ is in a higher row and hence earlier, and same-row or same-column swaps are excluded), while in different components $r$ is earlier exactly when its component is earlier. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 **Row sorting.** Let $S,T$ be $\mu$-tableaux with $S\unlhd T$; by steps 1.1 and 2.1 it suffices to treat a single transposition $S=(a\,b)T$ with $a<b$ and $b$ earlier than $a$ in $T$, the general case following by composing the finitely many single-swap comparisons. Write $S^+,T^+$ for the tableaux obtained by sorting every row increasingly. If $a,b$ share a row of $T$, then $S$ and $T$ have the same row sets and $S^+=T^+$. Otherwise the node of $b$ lies in a strictly earlier row than the node of $a$: they are in different rows by the previous sentence, and $b$ earlier than $a$ forces $b$'s row to be the earlier one. Entries other than $a,b$ occupy the same nodes in $S$ and $T$. For a value $c$, the prefix row lengths of $S^+$ and $T^+$ at $c$ are the rows' counts of entries $\le c$; if $c<a$ or $c\ge b$ these counts agree, while if $a\le c<b$ the count vector of $S^+$ is obtained from that of $T^+$ by moving one unit from the row of $a$ to the earlier row of $b$. Moving a unit to an earlier row raises every partial sum of the row sequence, so $\operatorname{sh}(S^{+\le c})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{+\le c})$ for every $c$; both tableaux are row-strict, so step 2.1 gives $S^+\unlhd T^+$. Hence $S\unlhd T$ implies $S^+\unlhd T^+$ in general. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]



4.1 **The vertical consecutive swap and its exceptional prefix.** Assume $\mu$ is a multipartition, $T$ standard, $r\downarrow_Tr+1$, so $r$ and $r+1$ occupy adjacent rows $a,a+1$ of one component in the same column $b$; the neighbour check of step 3.1 shows that $U:=s_rT$ is row-strict. Let $S$ be standard with $S\lhd U$; we prove $S\unlhd T$. By step 2.1, $\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le c})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le c})$ for all $c$, and for $c\ne r$ the tableaux $U^{\le c}$ and $T^{\le c}$ occupy the same nodes, so their shapes agree. For $c=r$ let $A_k$ be the number of entries $\le r-1$ in the first $k$ rows of $T$ (the same for $U$) and note that $\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})$ has row lengths $A_k-A_{k-1}+[k=a+1]$ while $\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le r})$ has $A_k-A_{k-1}+[k=a]$; thus $\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le r})$ is obtained from $\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})$ by moving one node from row $a+1$ up to row $a$. Because $T$ is standard, the node of $r$ in row $a$ has column $b$, so exactly $b-1$ entries of row $a$ lie in columns $<b$, all of them $\le r-1$, and the same count holds in row $a+1$ whose node in column $b$ is occupied by $r+1$; hence $A_a-A_{a-1}=b-1=A_{a+1}-A_a$ and the switch hypothesis $\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})_a-\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})_{a+1}=(b-1)-((b-1)+1)=-1$ holds. Lemma 3.1 of the source, proved here: if $\nu$ is a row sequence and $\nu_a-\nu_{a+1}=-1$, and $\hat\nu$ interchanges the two consecutive parts $\nu_a,\nu_{a+1}$, then $\hat\nu$ has the same partial sums as $\nu$ except at index $a$, where they are larger by one; consequently any multipartition $\lambda$ with $\lambda\unrhd\nu$ also satisfies $\lambda\unrhd\hat\nu$: if its partial sum at $a$ equalled that of $\nu$, the inequalities at $a-1$ and $a+1$ would force $\lambda_a\le\nu_a<\nu_{a+1}\le\lambda_{a+1}$, contradicting the weakly decreasing parts in that component. Thus its partial sum at $a$ is at least one larger; other partial sums are unchanged. Apply this with $\lambda=\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le r})$, $\nu=\operatorname{sh}(U^{\le r})$, $\hat\nu=\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le r})$: the row sequence of a standard tableau's prefix is a multipartition, and the computed switch identity verifies the hypothesis, so $\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le r})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le r})$. With the equalities for $c\ne r$, step 2.1 gives $S\unlhd T$. In the same-row case $r\to_Tr+1$ one has $T=U^+$ and $S=S^+$, so step 3.2 gives $S\unlhd T$ directly; this proves both clauses of the vertical exceptional-prefix fact. [step 2.1, step 3.2, algebra]

4.2 **The four terminal alternatives (horizontal).** Let $\mu$ be a multipartition and $T$ be standard with $r\to_Tr+1$. Consider the three properties: (a) there is $t$ with $|t-r|>1$ such that $t\nearrow_Tt+1$ or $t$ lies in a later component than $t+1$; (b) $r+1\nearrow_Tr+2$ or $r+1$ lies in a later component than $r+2$; (c) $r-1\nearrow_Tr$ or $r-1$ lies in a later component than $r$. By step 3.1 an incoming edge at $t$ (that is, $s_tT$ standard with $t$ earlier than $t+1$ in $s_tT$) is equivalent to $t\nearrow_Tt+1$ or $t$ in a later component than $t+1$. If (a) holds, then $X:=s_tT$ is standard and $X\xrightarrow{t}T$ is an edge, so $T$ is $t$-terminal, and since $t\notin\{r,r+1\}$ the relation $r\to_Tr+1$ persists in $X$; this is alternative (1). If (b) holds with $r+1\nearrow_Tr+2$, then in $X:=s_{r+1}T$ the entry $r+1$ occupies the higher node of $r+2$, so $X\xrightarrow{r+1}T$ is an edge; since $r,r+1$ are adjacent in one row and $r+2$ is above and right, $r+1$ is above and right of $r$ in $X$, so $Y:=s_rX$ is standard and $Y\xrightarrow{r}X$ is an edge with $r$ moving to the higher node, and in $Y$ the entries $r+1,r+2$ are adjacent in one row with $r+1$ to the left; this is alternative (2). If (b) holds with $r+1$ in a later component than $r+2$, the same construction with component arguments gives (2). If (c) holds, the mirror construction gives (3). It remains to observe that if none of (a),(b),(c) holds, then $T$ has no incoming edge: indeed (a) is exactly the incoming-edge alternative at any $t\notin\{r-1,r,r+1\}$, (c) at $t=r-1$, and (b) at $t=r+1$, while at $t=r$ both alternatives of step 3.1 fail because $r$ and $r+1$ lie in one row with $r$ to the left. A standard tableau with no incoming edge is $t^\mu$: if $T\ne t^\mu$, choose the least $t$ with the node of $t+1$ earlier than the node of $t$ in $T$ (such $t$ exists because otherwise the entries occur in the order $1,2,\dots,d$); then standardness forces $t\nearrow_Tt+1$ or an earlier component for $t+1$, so the incoming-edge alternative at $t$ holds and gives the existence of an edge into $T$, a contradiction. Hence in this final case $T=t^\mu$, which is alternative (4). [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 **The vertical terminal alternatives.** Let $\mu$ be a multipartition and $r\downarrow_Tr+1$ at $(a,b,n)$, so the two nodes are vertically adjacent. Use the following precise tests: (a) an incoming edge $t$ with $|t-r|>1$; (b) $r\nearrow_Tr+2$ or $r+1$ is in a later component than $r+2$; (c) $r-1\nearrow_Tr+1$ or $r-1$ is in a later component than $r$. Test (a) gives $s_tT\xrightarrow{t}T$ and preserves the vertical pair. In test (b), standardness and the consecutiveness of the three entries force $s_{r+1}T$ and $s_rs_{r+1}T$ to be standard: the node of $r+2$ is above and right of $r$, hence above and right of the node of $r+1$, and after the first swap the nodes of $r,r+1$ are incomparable. Thus $s_rs_{r+1}T\xrightarrow{r}s_{r+1}T\xrightarrow{r+1}T$, while $r+1,r+2$ occupy the original vertical pair in $s_rs_{r+1}T$. The different-component case uses the same two swaps without any within-component inequality. Test (c) gives the analogous $s_rs_{r-1}T\xrightarrow{r}s_{r-1}T\xrightarrow{r-1}T$, with $r-1,r$ in the original vertical pair. If none of the tests holds, labels other than the triple adjacent to $r$ cannot have an inversion between consecutive row-reading positions: any such inverse-order consecutive pair is in incomparable nodes or distinct components and is exactly an incoming edge. Reading $r-1,r-2,\ldots,1$ backwards and $r+2,r+3,\ldots,d$ forwards consequently places them in row-reading order except for the lower-row prefix before the vertical pair and the upper-row tail after it; tests (c) and (b) exclude any further excursion. More explicitly, if $L$ is the initial label at $(a,b,n)$ and $U$ the initial label at $(a+1,b,n)$, the forced belt filling is $L,\ldots,L+b-2$ in the first $b-1$ lower-row positions, $r=L+b-1$ in $(a,b,n)$, $r+1=L+b$ in $(a+1,b,n)$, and $L+b+1,\ldots,U$ in the remaining upper-row tail; all outside entries are unchanged. Among standard belt fillings this is Bruhat-maximal: the $b$ lower-row entries are the lexicographically smallest possible increasing subset, namely $L,\ldots,L+b-2,L+b$, because choosing the $b$ smallest would violate column $b$. Every other valid subset has no smaller prefix counts in the upper row, hence is below it by step 2.1. This is exactly the Garnir tableau, including $b=1=\mu_a$. A horizontal brick is a consecutive same-row string. All selections, chains and comparisons are finite, so no choice principle is used. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Generic nondegenerate local inverse tables on integer colors
items.statement:
Work over a field $k$ of characteristic zero, with $q\in k^\times$ of infinite multiplicative order, integer colors, and the arrows $a\to a+1$. On any finite permutation-stable set of color words, complete the dot ring at the zero dots. The completed local affine Hecke presentation at spectral words $(q^{i_1},\ldots,q^{i_d})$ and the completed type-$A_\infty$ KLR presentation have mutually inverse changes of generators below. This is a local statement; it does not assert cyclotomic support, a tower comparison, or a Specht dictionary.

Write $x=q^a(1-u)$, $z=q^b(1-v)$ and set
$$P_{ab}(u,v)=\begin{cases}1&a=b,\\(1-q)/(1-x/z)&a\ne b,\end{cases}$$
$$Q_{ab}(u,v)=\begin{cases}1-q+qv-u&a=b,\\-q^a/(x-z)&a=b+1,\\(x-qz)/(x-z)&a\ne b,\ a\ne b+1.\end{cases}$$
These are explicit, invertible, rank-independent power series over $k$; in particular the result applies over $\mathbb C$. Use $y_r=1-q^{-i_r}X_r$ on $e(i)$ and the source convention $\psi_r=-\tau_r$, where $\tau$ is the native crossing. The changes of generators are
$$\psi_re(i)=(T_r+P_{i_ri_{r+1}}(y_r,y_{r+1}))Q_{i_ri_{r+1}}(y_r,y_{r+1})^{-1}e(i),$$
$$X_re(i)=q^{i_r}(1-y_r)e(i),\qquad T_re(i)=(\psi_rQ_{i_ri_{r+1}}(y_r,y_{r+1})-P_{i_ri_{r+1}}(y_r,y_{r+1}))e(i).$$
The quadratic polynomial is $K_{aa}=0$, $K_{a,a+1}(u,v)=v-u$, $K_{a+1,a}(u,v)=u-v$, and $K_{ab}=1$ otherwise. Equal-color dot-sliding constants for $\psi$ are $+1$. The braid order is $\psi_1\psi_2\psi_1-\psi_2\psi_1\psi_2$; on $(a,b,a)$ its value is $[K_{ab}(u,v)-K_{ab}(w,v)]/(w-u)$, hence respectively $+1,-1,0$ for forward, backward, nonadjacent colors.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The integer-color local presentations just stated. Their coefficient ring is the direct sum of one formal power-series ring per color word; no finite-$e$ definition or comparison theorem is being instantiated. In the Hecke presentation the spectral idempotents are the projections to these local rings. Multiplication by $X_r$ on its $i$-summand is $q^{i_r}(1-y_r)$. The usual affine Hecke relations are $T_r^2=(q-1)T_r+q$, $T_rX_rT_r=qX_{r+1}$, and the braid and distant commutation relations.

## Proof

**Given:** The displayed presentations and the formal series $P,Q$.

1.1 All coefficients are legal. For $a\ne b$, $x-z$ has constant $q^a-q^b\ne0$. In the last case of $Q$, $x-qz$ has nonzero constant because $a\ne b+1$. In the backward case $-q^a/(x-z)$ is a unit. In the equal case $1-q\ne0$. Thus every denominator is a unit and each $Q$ is a unit. The formulas depend only on the adjacent pair, so they make sense in every rank and in every finite color window. [given, algebra]



1.2 Use an explicit polynomial representation. On the $i$-component let dots multiply, and let a permutation simultaneously permute coordinates and colors. With $\partial_r=(s_r-1)/(y_r-y_{r+1})$, define $\psi_r$ on an equal pair to be $\partial_r$; on an unequal source pair $(a,b)$ let its output in the swapped component be $h_{ab}(u,v)s_r$, where $h_{ab}(u,v)=v-u$ if $a=b+1$ and $h_{ab}=1$ otherwise. The equal-color quotient is a power series because the numerator vanishes on $u=v$. Its product rule is $\partial(fg)=\partial(f)g+(sf)\partial(g)$. Consequently $\partial v=u\partial+1$, $v\partial=\partial u+1$, and $\partial^2=0$. On unequal pairs the square is multiplication by $h_{ba}(u,v)h_{ab}(v,u)=K_{ab}(u,v)$. These computations verify all mixed and quadratic relations, including the native sign $\tau=-\psi$. [given, algebra]



2.1 Three distinct colors. In both three-crossing words the coefficient of the longest permutation is the product of the three pair factors, transported to the same coordinates. Each pair is crossed once. The factors commute and $s_1s_2s_1=s_2s_1s_2$, so the two words agree. This argument does not require nonadjacency; some of the factors can be linear. [step 1.2, algebra]



2.2 First two colors equal. For $(a,a,b)$ write $h=h_{ab}$. The left word is $h(u,v)h(u,w)s_1s_2\partial_1$, and the right word is $\partial_2h(u,v)h(u,w)s_1s_2$. The product of factors is invariant under swapping $v,w$, so its $\partial_2$ is zero. Also $\partial_2s_1s_2=s_1s_2\partial_1$ by conjugating the displayed quotient. The words agree. For $(a,b,b)$ the left word is $\partial_1h(v,w)h(u,w)s_2s_1$, and the right word is $h(v,w)h(u,w)s_2s_1\partial_2$. Here the product is invariant under swapping $u,v$, and $\partial_1s_2s_1=s_2s_1\partial_2$. This verifies the third color pattern separately. [step 1.2, algebra]



2.3 Outer colors equal. On $(a,b,a)$ with $a\ne b$, put $h=h_{ab}$ and $g=h_{ba}$. Expanding the one equal-color crossing gives left and right words $\frac{g(u,v)}{u-w}\bigl(h(v,w)s_1s_2s_1-h(v,u)\bigr),\qquad\frac{h(v,w)}{u-w}\bigl(g(u,v)s_2s_1s_2-g(w,v)\bigr).$ Their longest-permutation terms cancel. Their difference is $[K_{ab}(w,v)-K_{ab}(u,v)]/(u-w)$, the stated braid correction. This equals $1$ when $b=a+1$, $-1$ when $a=b+1$, and zero otherwise. Thus the apparent denominator cancels identically. [step 1.2, algebra]



2.4 All three colors equal. Put $D=(u-v)(u-w)(v-w)$. Expanding the quotients and collecting each of the six permutations gives $\partial_1\partial_2\partial_1=\partial_2\partial_1\partial_2=-D^{-1}\sum_{t\in S_3}\operatorname{sgn}(t)t.$ The numerator is alternating and hence divisible by each of the three pair differences, so this is an operator on power series. This explicitly supplies the all-equal case omitted as an exercise in the source. Together with steps 2.1–2.3 it proves all five braid patterns. [step 1.2, algebra]



2.5 Compute the Hecke generators in the same representation. At an output component set $U=X_r$, $V=X_{r+1}$. For unequal colors the swapped input series $Q$ times $h$ is $(qU-V)/(U-V)$: in the backward case $qU-V=q^a(v-u)$, and the swapped input series is $-q^a/(V-U)=q^a/(U-V)$, so multiplying by $h=v-u$ gives exactly the stated coefficient. In every other unequal case this is the last row of $Q$ directly. Also $-P=(1-q)V/(U-V)$. For equal colors, expand $\partial Q-1$; its permutation coefficient is $(1-q+qu-v)/(u-v)$ and its identity coefficient is $-(1-q)(1-v)/(u-v)$. Thus in every case $T_r=A(U,V)s_r+B(U,V),\qquad A(U,V)=\frac{qU-V}{U-V},\quad B(U,V)=\frac{(1-q)V}{U-V}.$ The equal-color poles cancel on power series, as follows already from $T=\partial Q-1$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]



3.1 Mixed and quadratic Hecke identities. Write $A_{ij}=A(X_i,X_j)$ and $B_{ij}=B(X_i,X_j)$. Direct common-denominator expansion gives $B_{ij}+B_{ji}=q-1$, $A_{ij}=q-B_{ij}$, and $A_{ij}A_{ji}=q+(q-1)B_{ij}-B_{ij}^2$. Squaring $A_{ij}s+B_{ij}$ therefore gives $(q-1)T+q$. The identity $TX_i-X_{i+1}T=(1-q)X_{i+1}$ follows by cancellation of its permutation term. Combining this identity with the quadratic identity gives $TX_iT=qX_{i+1}$. Distant commutations follow from disjoint variables. [step 2.5, algebra]



4.1 The Hecke braid holds in every color pattern, including all equal. Set $c=q-1$. Clearing the three pair denominators gives the rational identity $B_{13}(c-B_{12}-B_{23})+B_{12}B_{23}=0$. The coefficients of the longest permutation, $s_1s_2$, and $s_2s_1$ in $T_1T_2T_1$ are $A_{12}A_{13}A_{23}$, $A_{12}A_{13}B_{23}$, and $B_{12}A_{23}A_{13}$; the right word has the same coefficients. The $s_1$ coefficients are $A_{12}(B_{13}B_{21}+B_{12}B_{23})$ and $A_{12}B_{23}B_{13}$; the displayed identity makes them equal. The $s_2$ comparison is its transposed version. The identity coefficients differ by $(B_{12}-B_{23})\bigl(B_{13}(c-B_{12}-B_{23})+B_{12}B_{23}\bigr)=0.$ This uses the quadratic product identity of step 3.1. These are all six permutations, so the braid is proved. It is a rational identity before any color specialization; the equal-color operators preserve power series by step 2.5. [step 2.5, step 3.1, algebra]



5.1 These operator checks imply presentation identities, rather than identities on a possibly nonfaithful module. For Hecke coefficients the relation is $T_rf=(s_rf)T_r+B(X_r,X_{r+1})(f-s_rf)$. It follows first on the Laurent generators from the affine mixed relation, then on products by its product rule, and on formal local coefficients by continuity. At equal colors $f-s_rf$ is divisible by $X_r-X_{r+1}$; at unequal colors that denominator is a unit. This also gives the spectral-idempotent relation by applying the same formula to the local projections. For KLR use its displayed divided-difference product rule. Thus in either presentation coefficients can be moved past crossings. A crossing word reduces to a chosen reduced word for a permutation: delete adjacent repeated simple reflections using the quadratic relation, and change reduced words using commuting and three-term braid moves. For KLR the braid correction has fewer crossings. Induction on crossing length therefore spans the algebra by coefficient multiples of one chosen word per permutation. The elementary adjacent-transposition sorting algorithm supplies the requisite Coxeter reductions. In the rational crossed-product action, each reduced word has a nonzero coefficient of its own permutation; all other terms have shorter permutation length. Distinct permutations are linearly independent over the rational function field: in a minimal nonzero relation of automorphisms, apply it to $fg$ and subtract one automorphism's value on $f$ times its application to $g$; choose a coordinate $f$ moved differently by two permutations to obtain a shorter relation, a contradiction. Color words in different output components are already independent. Hence the spanning words are independent and both actions are faithful. The argument extends to formal coefficients using their fraction fields and the same finite spanning words. [step 1.2, step 2.4, step 4.1, algebra]



6.1 Both directions and both composites. In the faithful KLR action, steps 2.5–4.1 prove the Hecke relations of the displayed inverse generators. In the faithful local Hecke action, solving step 2.5 gives precisely the polynomial crossings of step 1.2, whose relations were proved in steps 1.2 and 2.1–2.4. Since $Q$ is a unit, the two operator subalgebras generated by coefficients and their respective crossings coincide. Thus the presentations are isomorphic. On idempotents and dots the two composites are the identity by the spectral decomposition and $X_r=q^{i_r}(1-y_r)$. On crossings the composite is $(\psi_rQ-P+P)Q^{-1}=\psi_r$; on Hecke crossings it is $(T_r+P)Q^{-1}Q-P=T_r$. These are ordered products; no coefficient has been commuted past a crossing. This completes the local inverse comparison in both directions. [step 1.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

items.statement: Let $A_{\mathbb Z}$ be a finite free unital integer algebra with $A_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q\otimes A_{\mathbb Z}$, and let $K$ be any characteristic-zero field. Suppose a finite-dimensional graded cyclic $A_K$-module $S_K$, with specified homogeneous generator $z_K$, is obtained from a homogeneous integer cyclic presentation $S_{\mathbb Z}=A_{\mathbb Z}/I_{\mathbb Z}$ by scalar extension, carrying $1+I_{\mathbb Z}$ to $z_K$. Suppose $S_K$ has a nonzero simple head $D_K$, with its specified grading normalization. Then the pair consisting of $D_K$ and the line spanned by the image $v$ of $z_K$ descends to $\mathbb Q$. More precisely there is a graded quotient $D_{\mathbb Q}$ of $S_{\mathbb Q}$ and $v_{\mathbb Q}\ne0$ such that $K\otimes D_{\mathbb Q}\cong D_K$ carries $1\otimes v_{\mathbb Q}$ to $v$. Consequently $A_{\mathbb Z}v$ is free of rank $\dim_KD_K$. If $D_K$ is absolutely simple, every nonzero quotient map from the specified $S_K$ to the fixed normalized $D_K$ has generator image on this same line, up to $K^\times$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[thm-jacobson-radical-is-nilpotent-and-the-quotient-is-semisimple]] gives a nilpotent radical and semisimple quotient for every finite-dimensional algebra.

[F2] [[thm-wedderburn-artin-theorem]] and [[thm-simple-modules-over-semisimple-rings]] describe semisimple finite-dimensional algebras and their simples.

[F3] [[thm-schurs-lemma-for-modules]] applies to simple modules.

[F4] [[thm-irreducible-quotient-adjoins-a-root]] constructs a finite root field for a monic irreducible polynomial. A nonconstant characteristic polynomial has a monic irreducible factor by finite induction on degree.

[A1] The integer presentation is an explicit prerequisite, not asserted here for the existing Hecke Specht construction. Its identification must preserve the specified generator.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the statement and F1–F4. All constructions involve finite-dimensional spaces and finite root fields; no Axiom of Choice is used.

1.1 We prove the regular-trace radical criterion directly over ANY characteristic-zero field $F$, without a splitting field or algebraic closure. Let $B$ be a finite-dimensional $F$-algebra and $\beta_B(a,b)=\operatorname{Tr}_F(L_{ab}:B\to B)$. Every element of $J(B)$ is orthogonal to $B$, because its product with any element lies in the nilpotent radical and hence has nilpotent left multiplication and zero trace. Choose a finite composition series of the left regular module. F1–F2 give $B/J(B)\cong\prod_iM_{n_i}(D_i)$, where each $D_i$ is a finite-dimensional division algebra over $F$; every simple composition factor is its column module $D_i^{n_i}$. Additivity of trace along the composition series shows that on this quotient the pairing is $\sum_i m_i\operatorname{Tr}_F(\rho_i(X_iY_i):D_i^{n_i}\to D_i^{n_i})$, where $m_i$ is the positive integer multiplicity of the column module in the regular composition series. Every $m_i$ is positive because the regular quotient already contains the corresponding column module. For a nonzero entry $x_{ab}$ of a block $X_i$, choose $Y_i$ with its only nonzero entry $(b,a)$ equal to $x_{ab}^{-1}$, and set all other blocks of $Y$ to zero. The product $X_iY_i$ has exactly one nonzero diagonal entry, namely $1$ at position $a$. On the $F$-space $D_i^{n_i}$, its action therefore has trace $\dim_F D_i$; off-diagonal blocks contribute no trace. The full pairing on this $Y$ is $m_i\dim_FD_i\ne0$ in characteristic zero. Thus the quotient pairing is nondegenerate and $\ker\beta_B=J(B)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Apply step 1.1 over $F=\mathbb Q$ and $F=K$. The regular multiplication and trace matrices for $A_K$ are scalar extensions of those for $A_{\mathbb Q}$. Row reduction of a finite matrix commutes with field extension, so the kernels satisfy $\ker\beta_{A_K}=K\otimes\ker\beta_{A_{\mathbb Q}}$. The radical criterion gives $J(A_K)=K\otimes J(A_{\mathbb Q})$. This argument applies equally to nonsplit division factors and needs no separable splitting theorem. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Put $S_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q\otimes S_{\mathbb Z}$ and $D_{\mathbb Q}=S_{\mathbb Q}/J(A_{\mathbb Q})S_{\mathbb Q}$. Tensoring quotient presentations is right exact and $K/\mathbb Q$ is flat, so $K\otimes D_{\mathbb Q}=S_K/J(A_K)S_K$. This last quotient is precisely the semisimple head: $A_K/J(A_K)$ is semisimple, so the quotient is semisimple, while every simple quotient kills $J(A_K)S_K$. Equivalently, intersections of maximal submodules equal $J(A_K)S_K$, since the intersection of the maximal submodules of a finite semisimple module is zero. The assumed head is simple, so this quotient is $D_K$. Its rational precursor is nonzero and simple: a proper nonzero rational submodule would remain proper and nonzero after faithful scalar extension. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra]

2.2 The radical of a finite-dimensional $\mathbb Q$-graded algebra is homogeneous. Indeed all scaling automorphisms $a_d\mapsto t^d a_d$ preserve its characteristic ideal $J$, for $t\in\mathbb Q^\times$. If $a=\sum_{d\in E}a_d\in J$ with finite degree set $E$, take $t=2^j$ for $j=0,\ldots,|E|-1$. The resulting coefficient matrix $((2^d)^j)_{j,d}$ is Vandermonde in the pairwise distinct rational numbers $2^d$, hence invertible; each $a_d$ is a rational linear combination of elements of $J$. Thus $J(A_{\mathbb Q})S_{\mathbb Q}$ is homogeneous and $D_{\mathbb Q}$ has the required quotient grading. Put $v_{\mathbb Q}=z_{\mathbb Q}+J(A_{\mathbb Q})S_{\mathbb Q}$. It is nonzero: otherwise cyclicity would force $D_{\mathbb Q}=0$. The scalar-extension quotient isomorphism preserves the generator, and hence its image is exactly $v$, including its degree. Any prescribed normalization shift is imposed simultaneously on both modules. [step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 The orbit $A_{\mathbb Z}v_{\mathbb Q}$ is generated as an abelian group by the images of a finite integer basis of $A_{\mathbb Z}$. It is torsion-free because it is a subgroup of a rational vector space. Its rational span is $D_{\mathbb Q}$, by cyclicity, so its rank equals $\dim_{\mathbb Q}D_{\mathbb Q}=\dim_KD_K$. The generator-preserving scalar-extension isomorphism identifies this orbit with $A_{\mathbb Z}v$. A finitely generated torsion-free abelian group is free, which proves the lattice assertion. [step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 If a fixed normalized $D_K$ is absolutely simple, a nonzero map $S_K\to D_K$ is surjective and kills the radical. Since the head is already the simple $D_K$, such maps factor through its canonical quotient and differ by an invertible endomorphism of $D_K$. This endomorphism $f$ is scalar using a finite root-field construction. Its nonconstant characteristic polynomial has a monic irreducible factor; by F4 the corresponding quotient field $L/K$ supplies a root $\alpha$. The matrix $f_L-\alpha I$ has zero determinant and hence a nonzero kernel. Absolute simplicity makes $D_L$ simple, so this commuting endomorphism must be zero. Thus $f_L=\alpha I$, and any diagonal entry of the original $K$-matrix shows $\alpha\in K$. Thus every allowed generator image is a scalar multiple of the constructed image, and scaling the lattice preserves freeness and rank. No claim concerning an arbitrary vector in $D_K$ was used. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The characteristic-zero field, finite integer interval, multiset, presentations, completions and specified series in the Statement.

[F1] The native KLR presentation in [[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]] has the two equal-color dot moves for $\tau$, the quadratic polynomial $Q$, and the reversed-word braid numerator $[Q(u,v)-Q(w,v)]/(w-u)$. Replacing $\tau$ by $-\psi$ gives $\psi u-v\psi=-1$, $\psi v-u\psi=1$, and $\psi_1\psi_2\psi_1-\psi_2\psi_1\psi_2=[Q(u,v)-Q(w,v)]/(w-u)$ on colors $(a,b,a)$.

[F2] The degenerate affine Hecke generator presentation of [[def-degenerate-affine-hecke-algebra]] over $\mathbb C$ has the relations listed in the Statement; here that presentation defines the algebra over $k$, and its basis and faithful action are proved below. The generators $s_r$ permute positions; the distinct notation $\sigma_r$ below means actual permutation operators on polynomial or formal coefficient functions.

## Proof

**Given:** The data and conventions of the Statement, and [F1]–[F2].

1.1 The coefficient completions. A symmetric polynomial in the commuting $x$ is central: the mixed relation gives $s_rf=(\sigma_rf)s_r-(f-\sigma_rf)/(x_r-x_{r+1})$, first on monomials by induction, then on polynomials. A symmetric $f$ has zero correction. The fiber of the elementary symmetric polynomials over their values on $\beta$ consists exactly of the ordered permutations of $\beta$: the coordinates are roots with multiplicities of $\prod_{a\in\beta}(t-a)$. Its radical is the intersection of the finitely many corresponding maximal ideals, by the polynomial factorization and the fact that every coordinate satisfies this monic polynomial. The elementary-symmetric ideal and this radical have cofinal powers, since the fiber is finite dimensional and its radical nilpotent. Chinese remainders and completion therefore give $\mathcal B_\beta$ with local coordinates $x_r-\nu_r$. On the KLR side symmetric dot polynomials are central by [F1], and the same argument at the all-zero fiber shows that its coefficient completion is $\mathcal B_\beta$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Invertible tables. If $a\ne b$ the integer $a-b$ is a nonzero unit in $k$, so $z^{-1}$ exists as a formal geometric series. In the backward case $a=b+1$, $q=z^{-1}$ has constant $1$. In the other unequal cases $q=1-z^{-1}$ has constant $1-(a-b)^{-1}$, which could vanish only when $a-b=1$, already excluded. Equal colors give constant $1$. For unequal colors $p_{ba}(v,u)=-p_{ab}(u,v)$. Direct multiplication gives $q_{ab}(u,v)q_{ba}(v,u)=1-z^{-2}$ on nonadjacent colors; on a forward arrow it gives $-(z-1)/z^2=(1-z^{-2})/(v-u)$ since $z=-1+u-v$; on a backward arrow it gives $(z+1)/z^2=(1-z^{-2})/(u-v)$ since $z=1+u-v$. Thus $Q_{ab}q_{ab}\sigma(q_{ba})=1-p_{ab}^2$ in all unequal cases, with no division by a nonunit left unresolved. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 A concrete KLR action. On $\mathcal B_\beta$, dots multiply and idempotents project. Define $E_r=(\sigma_r-1)/(y_r-y_{r+1})$ on equal adjacent colors. The numerator is divisible by the denominator for polynomials and formal series, so $E_r$ preserves the coefficient algebra. For unequal source colors $(a,b)$ define $\psi_r(fe(\nu))=c_{ab}(y_r,y_{r+1})\sigma_r(f)e(s_r\nu)$, where $c_{ab}(u,v)=v-u$ if $a=b+1$ and $c_{ab}(u,v)=1$ otherwise. These explicit operators prove the local relations in the following five cases. [step 2.1, given, construct, algebra]

4.1 Quadratic and dot moves. Write $\delta=u-v$. On equal colors $E^2=0$, since $E(f)$ is invariant under $\sigma$, and $Eu-vE=-1$, $Ev-uE=1$ follow by expanding the numerator. On unequal colors the dot moves are permutation identities and $\psi^2=c_{ba}(u,v)c_{ab}(v,u)=Q_{ab}(u,v)$. Indeed these products are $v-u$ on a forward arrow, $u-v$ on a backward arrow, and $1$ off edges. Disjoint crossings commute because their variables and their two-color factors are disjoint. Idempotent moves and commutative dot relations hold by construction. [F1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Three distinct colors. Put $u=y_1,v=y_2,w=y_3$, $s=\sigma_1,t=\sigma_2$, $\rho=sts=tst$, $L=\psi_1\psi_2\psi_1$, $M=\psi_2\psi_1\psi_2$. On a source $(a,b,c)$ with all colors distinct, direct consecutive application of step 3.1 gives both $L(f)$ and $M(f)$ equal to $c_{bc}(u,v)c_{ac}(u,w)c_{ab}(v,w)\rho(f)$ in the $(c,b,a)$ summand. The three pair factors commute. Hence $L=M$ for every edge pattern among three distinct integer colors. [step 4.1, step 3.1, algebra]

6.1 Exactly the first two equal. On $(a,a,b)$, $a\ne b$, put $h=c_{ab}(u,v)c_{ab}(u,w)$. Consecutive application gives $L(f)=h\,stE_1(f)$ and $M(f)=E_2(h\,stf)$. The polynomial $h$ is symmetric in $v,w$, including the backward case $h=(v-u)(w-u)$, so the product rule $E_2(hg)=E_2(h)g+t(h)E_2(g)$ gives $M(f)=hE_2stf$. Finally $E_2st=stE_1$: both sides equal $(\rho-st)/(v-w)$, with the denominator transformed when the permutation lies to its left. Thus $L=M$. [step 5.1, step 3.1, algebra]

7.1 Exactly the last two equal. On $(a,b,b)$, $a\ne b$, put $h=c_{ab}(u,w)c_{ab}(v,w)$. The two words give $L(f)=E_1(h\,tsf)$ and $M(f)=h\,tsE_2(f)$. Here $h$ is symmetric in $u,v$, including $h=(w-u)(w-v)$ when $a=b+1$. The product rule gives $L(f)=hE_1tsf$. The identity $E_1ts=tsE_2=(\rho-ts)/(u-v)$ now yields $L=M$. This explicitly checks the second repeated-neighbor pattern. [step 6.1, step 3.1, algebra]

8.1 Equal outer colors. On $(a,b,a)$, $a\ne b$, full expansion of the single middle divided difference gives $L(f)=c_{ba}(u,v)[c_{ab}(v,w)\rho(f)-c_{ab}(v,u)f]/(u-w)$ and $M(f)=c_{ab}(v,w)[c_{ba}(u,v)\rho(f)-c_{ba}(w,v)f]/(u-w)$. The $\rho(f)$ terms cancel, and step 4.1 gives $(L-M)(f)=[Q_{ab}(w,v)-Q_{ab}(u,v)]f/(u-w)$. Thus the correction is $+1$ for $a\to b$, $-1$ for $a\leftarrow b$, and zero off edges. The displayed expressions have removable denominators because their original numerators come from divided differences; the final quotient is a polynomial. [step 7.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

9.1 All three equal. For $\Delta=(u-v)(u-w)(v-w)$, expand the three factors $E=(\sigma-1)/(\text{dot difference})$ in either order. Moving permutations to the right gives the complete identity $E_1E_2E_1=E_2E_1E_2=(\rho-st-ts+s+t-1)/\Delta$. For example the $\rho$ coefficient is $1/\Delta$, the $st$ and $ts$ coefficients are $-1/\Delta$, the $s,t$ coefficients are $1/\Delta$, and the identity coefficient is $-1/\Delta$. Both sides preserve formal series by their original divided-difference formulas, so this rational equality proves their equality without inverting dots in the algebra. This supplies the all-equal case omitted in the cited source. [step 8.1, step 3.1, algebra]

10.1 Faithfulness for the KLR action. Moving dots to the right using step 4.1, and replacing repeated crossings and braid differences using steps 5.1–9.1, spans the presented KLR algebra by $\psi_w f(y)e(\nu)$ for fixed reduced words $w$. Termination uses crossing length: every quadratic reduction or braid correction has smaller length; reduced words for a permutation are connected by the elementary symmetric-group braid moves. In the rational-function action each $\psi_w$ has leading term a nonzero coefficient times $w$, and all other terms have smaller permutation length. Distinct permutations of variables are linearly independent over the rational-function field: a shortest putative relation, evaluated on $fg$ minus one selected automorphism's value on $g$ times its evaluation on $f$, gives a shorter nonzero relation. Hence these spanning monomials are independent. The same triangular argument over fractions of formal series proves faithfulness of the completed action, whose elements are the finite sum over $w,\nu$ with formal coefficient $f$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, algebra]

11.1 Why formal extension is legitimate. There are finitely many $w,\nu$, and each basis vector $\psi_we(\nu)$ has a finite crossing degree. Symmetric positive-degree dots form a central ideal with powers cofinal with dot-degree powers in each coefficient algebra by step 1.1. The PBW module just proved is consequently finite free over its right coefficient algebra and completes coefficientwise. Multiplication extends continuously: moving a formal coefficient through a crossing uses a variable permutation or one divided difference, decreasing its order by at most one, so any finite product has a uniform finite order loss. The displayed completed PBW expansion is therefore the actual central completion, rather than an additional relation imposed on $R_\beta$. [step 1.1, step 10.1, algebra]

12.1 The common degenerate Hecke operator. In the fraction algebra set $Z_r=x_r-x_{r+1}$ and $S_r=(1+Z_r^{-1})\sigma_r-Z_r^{-1}$. On an unequal source component the diagonal term is $-z^{-1}f$, while its crossing coefficient on the target component is $1+(b-a+u-v)^{-1}$. On equal colors this operator is $\sigma_r-(1-\sigma_r)/(u-v)$ and preserves formal series. Thus $S_r$ acts on $\mathcal B_\beta$ in every case. All identities in the next two steps are computed in the fraction algebra and then hold for these regular operators. This use of auxiliary fractions does not assert that a dot difference is invertible in the completion or its quotients. [step 11.1, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

13.1 Hecke quadratic and mixed identities. Let $A=Z_r^{-1}$; then $\sigma_r(A)=-A$. Expanding $S_r^2$ gives identity coefficient $(1+A)(1-A)+A^2=1$ and crossing coefficient $(1+A)A-A(1+A)=0$. Thus $S_r^2=1$, including equal colors. In $S_rx_{r+1}-x_rS_r$ the crossing terms cancel and the diagonal term is $A(x_r-x_{r+1})=1$. Disjoint $S_r$ commute, and dots outside the pair commute with $S_r$. These are precisely the quadratic, mixed and far-commuting relations of [F2]. [F2, step 12.1, algebra]

14.1 Complete Hecke braid coefficients. In spectral variables put $Z=x_1-x_2$, $U=x_2-x_3$, $V=Z+U$, $A=Z^{-1}$, $B=U^{-1}$, $C=V^{-1}$. Both products $S_1S_2S_1$ and $S_2S_1S_2$ have coefficients, in permutation order $(1,s,t,st,ts,\rho)$, equal to $(-C-ABC,\ (1+A)BC,\ (1+B)AC,\ -B(1+A)(1+C),\ -A(1+B)(1+C),\ (1+A)(1+B)(1+C))$. To verify the reductions, multiply using $(f\sigma)(g\eta)=f\sigma(g)\sigma\eta$, $s(A)=-A$, $s(B)=C$, $t(B)=-B$, $t(A)=C$, and $AB=C(A+B)$. For example the raw $s$ coefficient in the first word is $A(1+A)(B-C)=(1+A)BC$; its raw identity coefficient is $-(1-A^2)C-A^2B=-C-ABC$. Interchanging $A,B$ and $s,t$ gives the second word's identical six coefficients. [step 13.1, step 12.1, algebra]

15.1 All five reverse braid cases. Step 14.1 is a rational identity in independent spectral variables, before assigning colors. Substitute $(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(a+u,b+v,c+w)$ on each source component and apply the color-permuting operators. It proves the full Hecke braid separately on $(a,b,c)$ with all distinct, $(a,a,b)$, $(a,b,b)$, $(a,b,a)$ and $(a,a,a)$, because each is the restriction of the same six-coefficient identity and every $S_r$ preserves $\mathcal B_\beta$ by step 12.1. Even when a displayed spectral denominator has zero constant, cancellation occurs in the original regular operators, and injectivity into fractions preserves the equality. Thus the all-equal reverse case also has a complete coefficient computation. [step 12.1, step 14.1, algebra]

16.1 Faithfulness for the Hecke action. The mixed relation moves polynomials to the right of $s$-words and the exact symmetric-group relations reduce each word to $s_w$, so $H_n^{\mathrm{dg}}$ is spanned by $s_wf(x)$. In the action of steps 12.1–15.1 its leading permutation coefficient is the product of nonzero rational factors $1+Z^{-1}$ along a reduced word. All lower terms have shorter permutation length. The shortest-relation argument of step 10.1 proves independence and therefore the affine Hecke PBW basis. Completing at the central ideal of step 1.1 gives the finite coefficientwise PBW module $\sum_{w,\nu}s_w k[\![y]\!]e(\nu)$; its operator action remains faithful by the same argument over formal fractions. The coefficients $1+Z^{-1}$ need only be nonzero in that field, not units in the coefficient ring. [F2, step 1.1, step 10.1, step 13.1, step 15.1, algebra]

17.1 Comparing the explicit tables. On an unequal source $(a,b)$, $S_r+p_{ab}$ has only the crossing term. Its target coefficient is $1+\zeta^{-1}$, where $\zeta=b-a+u-v$. Right multiplication by $q_{ab}^{-1}$ substitutes $(v,u)$ on that target. If $a\to b$, $q_{ab}(v,u)=1+\zeta^{-1}$, giving coefficient $1$; if $a\leftarrow b$, $q_{ab}(v,u)=-\zeta^{-1}$ and $\zeta=-1+u-v$, giving coefficient $-(\zeta+1)=v-u$; off edges the quotient is again $1$. On equal colors $S_r=\sigma_r-(1-\sigma_r)/(u-v)$, and $(S_r+1)(1+v-u)^{-1}=(\sigma_r-1)/(u-v)=E_r$ by moving the inverse through $\sigma_r$. Thus $(S_r+p)q^{-1}=\psi_r$ in the faithful action. Equivalently $\psi_rq-p=S_r$. [step 16.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 12.1, algebra]

18.1 Homomorphisms in both directions. Faithfulness in steps 10.1–11.1 and 16.1 transfers the concrete equalities to the completed presented algebras. Step 17.1 identifies the forward images with the operators checked in steps 4.1–9.1, so all KLR relations hold in $\widehat H_\beta^{\mathrm{dg}}$. It identifies the reverse images with the operators checked in steps 13.1–15.1, so all Hecke relations hold in $\widehat R_\beta$. The coefficient-algebra maps identify the central completion topologies: the symmetric ideal vanishing at the spectral multiset and the all-zero dot ideal have cofinal powers on $\mathcal B_\beta$ by step 1.1. Therefore the maps extend continuously to the stated completions. This proves both directions locally rather than importing a cyclic finite-$e$ theorem. [step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, step 8.1, step 9.1, step 11.1, step 13.1, step 15.1, step 16.1, step 17.1, construct]

19.1 Inverse composites and uniformity. The coefficient maps fix every $e(\nu)$ and invert $y_r=x_r-\nu_r$ componentwise. The crossing composites are $(\psi_rq-p+p)q^{-1}=\psi_r$ and $((s_r+p)q^{-1})q-p=s_r$, with the same right multiplication order. Hence each composite is the identity on its generators, coefficient series and completion. None of $p,q,c$ depends on the rank, multiset, interval endpoints, level or cyclotomic charge, so enlarging an interval preserves every formula on the old tuples. Nilpotent dots permit finite evaluation of series, and every proved identity survives a quotient. Rank zero has coefficient algebra $k$ and both maps are the identity; empty positive-rank sectors have zero algebra. No assertion about cyclotomic support, based Grothendieck classes or Specht modules is needed for this local comparison. [step 18.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Generic cyclotomic type-A support is bounded by rank
items.statement:
Let $k$ have characteristic zero, let $\xi\in k^\times$ have infinite
multiplicative order, and fix a finite integral multicharge
$m_1,\ldots,m_\ell$. Write $S=\{m_j:1\le j\le\ell\}$.
Use the arbitrary-base presentations of
[[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]] to define
$H_d^{\deg}$ by $\prod_j(x_1-m_j)=0$ and $H_d^{\xi}$ by
$\prod_j(X_1-\xi^{m_j})=0$.
For $d>0$, every nonzero joint generalized weight in the regular module has
labels $\nu\in\mathbb Z^d$, with eigenvalues $\nu_r$ respectively
$\xi^{\nu_r}$, and
$$\min_{s\in S}|\nu_r-s|\le d-1.$$
Thus both algebras have finite joint spectral decompositions defined over $k$.

Use the directed line $i\to i+1$ on $\mathbb Z$, with $d_i=1$,
$Q_{i,i+1}(u,v)=v-u$, $Q_{i+1,i}(u,v)=u-v$ and $Q_{ij}=1$ for
$|i-j|>1$. Define the rank-$d$ cyclotomic KLR algebra as the direct sum of its
finite-content presentations, with first-strand exponents
$\lambda_i=\#\{j:m_j=i\}$. Every nonzero word idempotent satisfies the same
bound, so this rank algebra is a finite sum of finite-dimensional graded
content algebras. Any interval containing
$[\min S-d+1,\max S+d-1]$ gives exactly the same rank-$d$ algebra;
enlarging it introduces only zero word idempotents. Rank zero is $k$.
At level zero every positive rank is zero. This lemma supplies support and
finite windows; it asserts no Hecke--KLR isomorphism or basis correspondence.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The presentations and parameters of the Statement.

[F1] The arbitrary monic cyclotomic Hecke quotients are finite-dimensional by
[[lem-cyclotomic-hecke-bounded-ordered-monomials-span]]. Their mixed and
quadratic relations are those of
[[def-type-a-affine-presentations-and-charged-cyclotomic-quotients]].

[F2] In the KLR presentation, a crossing between distant colors has square
$1$ and interchanges their word idempotents
([[def-quiver-hecke-klr-algebra-for-a-symmetrizable-cartan-datum]]).
On any finite color interval, homogeneous cyclotomic content algebras are
finite-dimensional with nilpotent dots
([[lem-cyclotomic-klr-dot-annihilators-and-finite-root-strings]]).

## Proof

1.1 Work over a finite splitting extension for the finitely many minimal polynomials of the commuting polynomial generators in the finite regular module of [F1]. Simultaneous primary decomposition gives joint generalized eigenspaces. On such a weight, the first value is a charge root, because the first cyclotomic polynomial annihilates the module. In the degenerate case connect distinct values differing by $1$; in the nondegenerate case connect distinct nonzero values whose ratio is $\xi$ or $\xi^{-1}$. This defines a graph on the distinct values in each word, with at most $d$ vertices. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For a KLR word, form the induced line graph on its distinct colors. If a component contains no charge, move its first occurrence left across all earlier letters. These letters lie in other components, so their color differences exceed $1$; [F2] makes every crossing invertible. The resulting word idempotent is nonzero if the original was, but its first color has exponent zero, so the cyclotomic relation kills it. This contradiction shows that each component contains a charge. A component with at most $d$ vertices is an interval, and every color has distance at most $d-1$ from a charge in that component. [F2, given, algebra]

2.1 The mixed relations give intertwiners $\theta_r=s_r(x_r-x_{r+1})+1$ and $\Theta_r=T_r(1-X_rX_{r+1}^{-1})+1-\xi$. Direct multiplication gives $\theta_r^2=1-(x_r-x_{r+1})^2$ and $\Theta_r^2=(1-\xi X_{r+1}X_r^{-1})(1-\xi X_rX_{r+1}^{-1})$; they interchange the two polynomial generators and commute with the others. For example $s_r(x_r-x_{r+1})=-(x_r-x_{r+1})s_r-2$, which yields the first square identity; the second follows by inserting $T_r^2=(\xi-1)T_r+\xi$ and $T_rX_rT_r=\xi X_{r+1}$. Between values in different graph components these squares have nonzero constant terms, hence are invertible on the generalized weight space. Each intertwiner therefore gives an isomorphism onto the swapped generalized weight space. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Suppose a component contains no charge root. Its earliest occurrence in the word can be moved to the first position by the invertible swaps of step 2.1: every preceding value belongs to a different component. The resulting nonzero weight space has an uncharged first value, contradicting the first cyclotomic relation. Consequently each component contains a charge root. A simple path from that root to any vertex has length at most $d-1$, so the value is an integer within $d-1$ of an integral charge, respectively a power $\xi^a$ with $|a-m_j|\le d-1$. Infinite order of $\xi$ makes the integer labels unique. All spectral values therefore belong to $k$, and their polynomial primary projectors descend to $k$ by the Chinese remainder identity. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Only finitely many words satisfy this bound. In every content presentation the generators and relations use only colors already present in that content, so replacing the full line by a finite interval containing the bound changes none of these presentations. All omitted contents have zero word idempotents by step 1.2. On the finite interval [F2] supplies finite-dimensionality and nilpotent dots, and the finite sum is finite-dimensional. This identifies the full rank algebra with each sufficiently large finite window, including compatibility of larger windows on the same generators. At level zero the first exponent is always zero, killing every positive-rank word; the Hecke polynomial is $1$ and gives the same zero quotient. Rank zero is the ground field by definition. No basis correspondence or Hecke--KLR inverse map has been used. [step 3.1, step 1.2, F1, F2, given] ∎

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The parameters, presentations, and the following two explicit
conditional inputs.

[A1] [[lem-generic-cyclotomic-type-a-support-is-bounded-by-rank]] supplies the support input: the algebras in rank $d>0$ are finite-dimensional, their dots are
nilpotent, and every surviving color lies in
$B_d=[\min S-d+1,\max S+d-1]\cap\mathbb Z$. Hecke joint spectral
projectors $e_H(\nu)$ exist over $k$, with eigenvalues $\nu_r$ or
$\xi^{\nu_r}$. The full-line KLR rank algebra is unchanged by any finite
interval containing $B_d$. At level zero all positive ranks are zero and
rank zero is $k$.

[A2] There are fixed pairwise formal series $p_{ab},q_{ab},P_{ab},Q_{ab}$
for every $a,b\in\mathbb Z$, independent of rank, multicharge, content and
window; $q_{ab},Q_{ab}$ are units. On every finite integer window, the local
replacements displayed in the Statement satisfy all affine mixed,
quadratic, distant and braid relations in both directions, with the same
KLR convention. This input is supplied locally by
[[lem-integer-color-degenerate-hecke-klr-local-inverse-tables]] and
[[lem-generic-nondegenerate-local-inverse-tables]], including all five equality
patterns of three colors in the same native convention $\psi=-\tau$; the
cited article and a finite-$e$ instantiation do not replace these local proofs. The first direction
uses the actual Hecke joint projectors and dots; the reverse uses the KLR
word idempotents and dots. No cyclotomic relation, inverse composite,
spectral identification or tower assertion is assumed in this input.

## Proof

1.1 Evaluate a formal series in commuting nilpotent dots by its finite Taylor sum. This evaluation is independent of the nilpotence exponent chosen: every larger truncation differs only by zero monomials. A series with nonzero constant term is a unit by a terminating geometric expansion. Thus all replacements in the Statement are defined. By [A1] only finitely many words survive in any rank. The local relation verifications in [A2], applied on those words, give homomorphisms between the affine presentations before checking the first-strand quotient. No cyclic wraparound or reduction of integer colors is used. [A1, A2, algebra]

2.1 On a first color $i$, write the degenerate cyclotomic polynomial as $f(i+y)=y^{\lambda_i}U_i(y)$, where $U_i(y)=\prod_{m_j\ne i}(i-m_j+y)$. Its constant term is nonzero in characteristic zero. In the other branch $g(\xi^i(1-y))=(-\xi^i)^{\lambda_i}y^{\lambda_i}V_i(y)$, where $V_i(y)=\prod_{m_j\ne i}(\xi^i-\xi^{m_j}-\xi^iy)$. Infinite multiplicative order makes its constant term nonzero. Both auxiliary factors are units after nilpotent evaluation. Thus the Hecke cyclotomic relation on each projector is equivalent to $y_1^{\lambda_i}e(i,\ldots)=0$. If $\lambda_i=0$, the unit polynomial kills the entire projector. This proves the cyclotomic factorization and descent in both directions. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Denote the descended reverse map by $\sigma_d:H_d\to R_d^\lambda$. On $e_R(\nu)R_d^\lambda$, each $\sigma_d(x_r)$ has sole generalized eigenvalue $\nu_r$, or $\sigma_d(X_r)$ has sole generalized eigenvalue $\xi^{\nu_r}$. Distinct colors have distinct values, and the orthogonal word idempotents sum to one. The simultaneous primary projector is therefore precisely left multiplication by $e_R(\nu)$. The Hecke polynomial projector maps to this idempotent: its Chinese-remainder polynomial is one modulo the corresponding primary factors and zero modulo all other factors. Hence $\sigma_d(e_H(\nu))=e_R(\nu)$. The forward map already sends $e_R(\nu)$ to $e_H(\nu)$. [A1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Both composites fix the word projectors by step 3.1 and the dots by direct substitution $x_r-\nu_r=y_r$, or $1-\xi^{-\nu_r}X_r=y_r$. On a word, the crossing composite is $(\psi_rq_{ab}-p_{ab}+p_{ab})q_{ab}^{-1}=\psi_r$, or $(\psi_rQ_{ab}-P_{ab}+P_{ab})Q_{ab}^{-1}=\psi_r$. Conversely the Hecke composite sends $s_re_H(\nu)$ to $((s_r+p_{ab})q_{ab}^{-1}q_{ab}-p_{ab})e_H(\nu)=s_re_H(\nu)$; the formula with $T,P,Q$ is identical. The polynomial generators are fixed, and the units $X_r^{-1}$ are fixed because inverses are unique. Thus the homomorphisms are inverse on every generator, without commuting a crossing through its series. [step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For ranks through $D>0$ at positive level use the common interval $W_D=[\min S-D,\max S+D]\cap\mathbb Z$. It contains the support through rank $D$ and one unused ghost color beyond each endpoint of $B_D$. A crossing permutes existing colors and never creates one; nevertheless these endpoint colors keep every boundary edge of a surviving color represented by the integer-line convention. For operations reaching rank $D+t$, use $W_{D+t}$, and enlarge further to contain any specified color and its neighbors. All extra word idempotents vanish by [A1]. Since [A2] fixes the same series for each ordered pair in every interval, evaluation on surviving words is unchanged by enlargement. The resulting maps are independent of windows and glue across all finite rank bounds. [A1, A2, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Let $\iota_H:H_d\to H_{d+1}$ send each existing Hecke generator to the generator with the same index. It is a homomorphism because all rank-$d$ relations, including the first-strand relation, hold in rank $d+1$. Its spectral projector satisfies $\iota_H(e_H(\nu))=\sum_a e_H(\nu,a)$: the first $d$ polynomial generators give a representation of $H_d$ on the rank-$d+1$ regular module, so their primary projector is the sum of exactly these joint projectors. Prefixes violating rank-$d$ support are zero by [A1] applied to this representation. This argument also holds for $d=0$, where the empty projector is one. [A1, given, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Define $\iota_R=\sigma_{d+1}\iota_H\phi_d$. The established inverse maps make this a homomorphism. Steps 3.1 and 6.1 give $\iota_R(e_R(\nu))=\sum_a e_R(\nu,a)$. The unchanged polynomial generators give the usual prefix dots. For $r<d$, the rank-independent pair series in [A2] and cancellation in step 4.1 give $\iota_R(\psi_re_R(\nu))=\sum_a\psi_re_R(\nu,a)$. These are exactly the standard right-appending KLR maps, so the individually constructed isomorphisms commute with the actual tower maps. Injectivity of the tower maps is neither needed nor inferred. [A2, step 4.1, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 Put $\epsilon_i^R=\sum_\nu e_R(\nu,i)$ in rank $d+1$, and define $\epsilon_i^H$ by the analogous spectral sum. Step 3.1 gives $\phi_{d+1}(\epsilon_i^R)=\epsilon_i^H$. Each last-color projector commutes with every prefix generator, since prefix crossings permute only the first $d$ colors and prefix dots preserve all colors. On left modules color restriction is $N\mapsto\epsilon_iN$, with the rank-$d$ action through its prefix map. Color induction is $M\mapsto A_{d+1}\epsilon_i\otimes_{A_d}M$. Step 7.1 identifies both prefix actions, and the algebra isomorphism identifies these induction bimodules on both sides. Explicitly $a\epsilon_i\otimes m\mapsto\phi_{d+1}(a)\epsilon_i\otimes m$ is a balanced bijection, with inverse obtained from $\sigma_{d+1}$. Restriction agrees by the same projector equality. These formulas are natural in module maps. [step 3.1, step 7.1, construct]

9.1 Composing the two comparisons through the same $R_d^\lambda$ proves the claimed degenerate/nondegenerate tower equivalence. Naturality from step 8.1 intertwines repeated induction and restriction, while step 5.1 covers every specified finite rank cut. At level zero use the identity on rank zero and the unique maps between zero algebras in positive rank; the sole map from rank zero to rank one is the map to zero, and all positive-rank functors vanish. Thus all ranks and levels are included. Every conclusion remains conditional on [A1] and [A2]; no local table identity or based theorem has been established by this gluing proof. [A1, step 5.1, step 8.1] ∎

coordinate functional** $\operatorname{Std}_\mu$ in the restricted integral

nondegenerate; identify its field dual with $V$ via $B$ and denote by

If $G^*(\lambda)$ is the $B$-dual upper vector, then

items.title: Graded module and projective Grothendieck groups of the KLR and Hecke towers
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field and let $R=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_+}R_\alpha$ be a tower of
finite-dimensional unital $\mathbb Z$-graded $k$-algebras with local units
$e(\alpha)$: every finite root-supported element has a unit given by the sum of its finitely many sector units, each
$R_\alpha$ a direct summand and $R_0=k$. Define
$$K_0^{\rm gr}(R):=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_+}K_0^{\rm gr}(R_\alpha),\qquad G_0^{\rm gr}(R):=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_+}G_0^{\rm gr}(R_\alpha),$$
the restricted direct sums of the blockwise Grothendieck groups of
[[def-graded-grothendieck-group-shift-module-and-cartan-map]]:
$K_0^{\rm gr}(R_\alpha)$ of finitely generated graded left
$R_\alpha$-projectives modulo split exact sequences
([[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]]) and
$G_0^{\rm gr}(R_\alpha)$ of finite-dimensional graded left $R_\alpha$-modules
modulo short exact sequences. Both are modules over
$A:=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ by $q[M]:=[M\{1\}]$
([[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]]), and inside each
finite-dimensional block the shift-orbit bases of
[[thm-graded-projective-and-simple-classes-have-shift-orbit-bases]] hold. The
Cartan homomorphism $c:K_0^{\rm gr}(R)\to G_0^{\rm gr}(R)$, $[P]\mapsto[P]$, is
$A$-linear. The forgetful maps $\zeta$ to the ungraded groups $K_0(R)$,
$G_0(R)$ are additive and satisfy $\zeta(qm)=\zeta(m)$. The groups $K_0^{\rm gr}$ and
$G_0^{\rm gr}$ are DIFFERENT objects and are never identified.

**The two towers used below.** (i) For the standard homogeneous cyclotomic
quotient of [[def-cyclotomic-klr-quotient-at-a-dominant-weight]] at the
level-one weight $\Lambda_0$ of
[[def-type-a-cyclotomic-specialization-of-the-qg-klr-algebras]], put
$R^\Lambda_\alpha=R^\Lambda(\alpha)$; every block is finite dimensional and has
the homogeneous symmetrizing functional of
`thm-cyclotomic-klr-algebras-are-finite-dimensional-graded-symmetric`, with
grading shifts as in [[def-klr-grading-and-diagrammatic-composition]]. (ii) For
the cyclotomic Hecke tower $H^{\Lambda}:=\bigoplus_\alpha H^\Lambda_\alpha$ of
`def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras` with the block decomposition
of `def-residue-sequence-idempotents-and-cyclotomic-hecke-blocks`, fix an
admissible local normalising series and transport the homogeneous KLR
decomposition through the blockwise isomorphism of
`thm-brundan-kleshchev-blockwise-hecke-klr-isomorphism`, as in
`cor-cyclotomic-hecke-blocks-inherit-a-nontrivial-z-grading`; the induced
transport identifies $K_0^{\rm gr}(H^{\Lambda})\cong K_0^{\rm gr}(R^\Lambda)$
as $A$-modules and similarly for $G_0^{\rm gr}$, compatibly with $\zeta$ and
with the Cartan homomorphisms. Every class has finite root support, so the
direct sums are restricted.

No choice principle is used in this definition.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $k$, a tower $R=\bigoplus_\alpha R_\alpha$ of
finite-dimensional graded algebras with local units over the standard
cyclotomic quotient at $\Lambda_0$, and the Hecke tower $H^\Lambda$ with an
admissible local normalising series. All modules are left modules and all maps
preserve degree.

[F1] For a finite-dimensional graded algebra $A$, the groups
$G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)$ and $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)$, the shift action
$v^r[M]=[M\{r\}]$ and the graded Cartan homomorphism
$c_A^{\mathrm{gr}}:[P]\mapsto[P]$ are those of
[[def-graded-grothendieck-group-shift-module-and-cartan-map]]; shift is
invertible and composes by addition of degrees, and $c_A^{\mathrm{gr}}$ is
$\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-linear.

[F2] The graded-simple shift orbits and the classes of chosen graded
projective covers form $\mathbb Z[v,v^{-1}]$-bases of
$G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)$ and $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(A)$ for every finite-dimensional
graded $k$-algebra $A$, with no positivity assumption
([[thm-graded-projective-and-simple-classes-have-shift-orbit-bases]]).

[F3] A finitely generated graded projective module is a finite direct sum of
finite-dimensional indecomposable graded projectives
([[def-finitely-generated-graded-projective-module]]), and internal shift is
the degreewise operation $M\{r\}_d=M_{d-r}$ of
[[def-graded-ring-module-bimodule-and-internal-shift]].

[F4] The cyclotomic quotient $R^\Lambda(\beta)$ at a dominant integral weight
is the quotient of the KLR algebra $R(\beta)$ by the two-sided ideal generated
by the first-strand cyclotomic elements, with local units $e(\beta)$ acting as
the identity on their summand
([[def-cyclotomic-klr-quotient-at-a-dominant-weight]]), and its grading is the
diagrammatic grading of
[[def-klr-grading-and-diagrammatic-composition]].

[F5] Every block $R^\Lambda(\alpha)$ of the standard level-one cyclotomic
quotient is finite dimensional and carries a homogeneous symmetrizing
functional (the blockwise finite-dimensionality and symmetry statement of
`thm-cyclotomic-klr-algebras-are-finite-dimensional-graded-symmetric`), and
the blockwise isomorphism of
`thm-brundan-kleshchev-blockwise-hecke-klr-isomorphism` matches each Hecke
block with its KLR block, the transported grading being supplied by
`cor-cyclotomic-hecke-blocks-inherit-a-nontrivial-z-grading`.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 **Restricted sums are A-modules.** Each summand $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(R_\alpha)$ is a module over $A$ by $q[P]=[P\{1\}]$, and shift by an integer $r$ sends a class concentrated in degree $\alpha$ to the same root degree $\alpha$, because internal shift changes only the internal grading and not the idempotent label [F1, F3]. Hence every finite $A$-combination of classes lives in finitely many root summands and the restricted direct sums are $A$-modules; the local units $e(\alpha)$ make each $R_\alpha$ a unital subalgebra and annihilate the other summands, so the restricted direct sum is well defined and no infinite-support class is introduced. [F1, F3]

1.2 **The maps c and zeta.** On each block the ungraded forgetful map sends a graded projective class to its underlying projective class and a graded module class to its underlying module class; it is additive, well defined on the defining relations, and satisfies $\zeta(q[M])=\zeta([M\{1\}])=[M]_{\rm ungr}=\zeta([M])$ [F1]. The graded Cartan homomorphism is the sum of the blockwise maps $[P]\mapsto[P]$, which are $A$-linear because including a projective into the module category commutes with internal shift; compatibility with $\zeta$ is immediate from the definitions. [F1]

1.3 **The KLR tower.** For the standard level-one cyclotomic quotient every block $R^\Lambda(\alpha)$ is finite dimensional and carries the homogeneous symmetrizing functional of [F5], so the shift-orbit bases of [F2] apply blockwise without any positivity hypothesis [F4, F5]. Since the root degree is additive, a finite combination of block classes has finite support and belongs to the restricted direct sum. [F2, F4, F5]

1.4 **Transport to the Hecke tower.** For each residue-content block, the blockwise theorem of [F5] gives a graded $k$-algebra isomorphism $\varphi_\alpha:H^\Lambda_\alpha\to R^\Lambda(\alpha)$ matched with the chosen admissible normalising series, and the inherited grading of [F5] makes $\varphi_\alpha$ homogeneous. Restriction of scalars along $\varphi_\alpha$ sends graded $R^\Lambda(\alpha)$-modules to graded $H^\Lambda_\alpha$-modules and is an equivalence of graded module categories: it is exact because it is induced by an algebra isomorphism, it preserves finite-dimensional modules, and it preserves projectives because restriction along an isomorphism has the exact quasi-inverse given by restriction along $\varphi_\alpha^{-1}$, which is also exact. Hence it induces group isomorphisms $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(H^\Lambda)\cong K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(R^\Lambda)$ and $G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(H^\Lambda)\cong G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(R^\Lambda)$; these are $A$-linear because a homogeneous isomorphism carries $M\{1\}$ to $M\{1\}$, and they intertwine the Cartan maps and the forgetful maps $\zeta$ with the ungraded identifications. [F1, F3, F5]

2.1 **The groups remain distinct and no choice is used.** The identification $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(R)\cong K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}(R^\Lambda)$ is only a module transport inside one of the two groups; the Cartan homomorphism $c$ and the forgetful $\zeta$ are not inverted or identified, and no statement of the definition equates $K_0^{\mathrm{gr}}$ with $G_0^{\mathrm{gr}}$. All constructions use the finite block decompositions, the local units, and the explicit homogeneous algebra isomorphisms, so no choice principle is invoked. [F1, F5, given] ∎

items.title: The nondegenerate root-of-unity level-one Hecke regime
items.statement:
**Parameters.** Let $F$ be a field and $\xi\in F^\times$ with finite quantum
characteristic $e=e(F,\xi)\in\{2,3,\dots\}$
([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). We work in
the NONDEGENERATE branch $\xi\ne1$; then $\xi$ is a primitive $e$-th root of
unity in $F$, and all statements on this page live in one of the two
sub-branches: (C0) $\operatorname{char}F=0$, or (CP)
$\operatorname{char}F=p>0$ with $p\nmid e$. The Hecke parameter is written
$\xi$ here; it is the letter $q$ of `def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras`.

**Hecke side.** Fix the level-one fundamental weight $\Lambda_0$ of the cyclic
affine type-$A$ datum with all $d_i=1$ and charge $0$
([[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]). With the conventions of
`def-affine-and-cyclotomic-type-a-hecke-algebras`, $H^\Lambda_d=H_{F,\xi}(S_d)$
is the finite type-$A$ Hecke algebra $T_r^2=(\xi-1)T_r+\xi$
(`prop-cyclotomic-hecke-algebras-of-level-one-are-finite-hecke-algebras`), and
$H^\Lambda_\alpha=e_\alpha H^\Lambda_d$ are its residue-content blocks
(`def-residue-sequence-idempotents-and-cyclotomic-hecke-blocks`).

**KLR side.** Use the type-$A$ specialization $Q^A$ of
`def-type-a-cyclotomic-specialization-of-the-qg-klr-algebras` with the same $e$
and the STANDARD homogeneous first-strand cyclotomic quotient
$R^\Lambda_\alpha$ of [[def-cyclotomic-klr-quotient-at-a-dominant-weight]]: the
cyclotomic relation is $y_1^{\delta_{i_1,0}}e(i)=0$, induction appends on the
right, and the grading is $\deg e(i)=0$, $\deg y_r=2$,
$\deg\psi_re(i)=-a_{i_ri_{r+1}}$
([[def-klr-grading-and-diagrammatic-composition]]). The transported grading on
$H^\Lambda_\alpha$ uses a FIXED admissible local normalising series
(`cor-cyclotomic-hecke-blocks-inherit-a-nontrivial-z-grading`); a different
series gives a graded-isomorphic transported algebra via $\rho'\rho^{-1}$, and
the graded multiplicities studied below do not depend on the choice.

**Grading and Fock variables.** All grading shifts and all global-basis
polynomials are in the variable $q$, $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$. Thus
$\xi\in F^\times$ (the Hecke parameter) and $q$ (the grading variable) are
INDEPENDENT data; the phrase "Ariki's normalization $\xi=q^2$" is retained only
as the source dictionary of [Ariki 1996], whose Hecke parameters are powers of
a square, and no numerical relation or specialization between $\xi$ and $q$ is
imposed.

**Fock side.** Use the level-one symmetric model of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]]: charge
$0$, node residues $c-r$, standard vectors $M_\mu$ for ALL partitions $\mu$,
basic/restricted labels the $e$-restricted partitions
$RP_\alpha=\{\lambda:\lambda_a-\lambda_{a+1}<e,\ \operatorname{cont}(\lambda)=\alpha\}$,
empty component $B(\Lambda_0)$. For $\lambda\in RP$ the conjugate $\lambda'$ is
$e$-regular. Write $P(\nu)$ for the independently constructed ordinary
Dipper--James Specht module and $D_{\rm DJ}^{\nu}$ for its form quotient in
`thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell`. Define
$\theta(T_r)=(\xi-1)-T_r=-\xi T_r^{-1}$, the involutive sign automorphism of
[[lem-dj-bridge-sign-automorphism-and-star-dual]]. After converting right
modules to left modules through the star anti-involution, the intrinsic
restricted Murphy simple with label $\lambda$ is the $\theta$-pullback of
$D_{\rm DJ}^{\lambda'}$, not the untwisted ordinary module. This is an ungraded
convention dictionary. The pullback can move blocks: on the multiplicative
Jucys--Murphy elements $\theta(X_j)=X_j^{-1}$, so charge-zero residue content
is sent from $\alpha$ to $-\alpha$. Thus the ordinary module before pullback has
the conjugate content; no claim identifies it untwisted inside the same block.
At $\xi=1$ the separate specialization theorem
`cor-dj-bridge-specialization-and-composition-multiplicity-dictionary`
identifies $\theta$ with sign tensoring over every field; $\xi=1$ remains
outside the present nondegenerate regime.

No choice principle is used.
